ai.definition: Green hydrogen is produced through the electrolysis of water using electricity generated from renewable energy sources like wind or solar. This process splits water into its constituent elements—hydrogen and oxygen—without emitting any greenhouse gases.
ai.howItWorks: Electrolyzers use an electric current to split water molecules (H2O) into hydrogen and oxygen. The electrolysis process can be powered by renewable energy sources such as wind turbines or solar panels, making the production of green hydrogen sustainable and environmentally friendly.
ai.problemSolved: Addressing the challenge of decarbonizing heavy industry sectors and transportation that are difficult to electrify directly, while also reducing overall greenhouse gas emissions from industrial processes and fuel use.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves setting up electrolyzers capable of operating at high pressures and temperatures. These systems require precise control over temperature, pressure, and electrical current to ensure efficient operation and product purity.
ai.buildProcess: Construction typically includes site preparation, installation of renewable energy generation facilities (wind turbines or solar panels), and the setup of electrolyzer units. Infrastructure for hydrogen storage and transportation must also be established.
ai.costDrivers: High initial capital costs associated with setting up renewable energy systems and electrolyzers, as well as ongoing operational expenses like maintenance and energy procurement. Cost reductions are expected through economies of scale and technological advancements in both renewable technologies and electrolysis processes.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Growing adoption but still dependent on supportive policies and infrastructure development to achieve widespread deployment. Expected to see significant growth as more countries commit to net-zero emissions targets.
ai.regulation: Currently, regulations vary widely by region. Many governments are developing frameworks that incentivize green hydrogen production through tax credits, grants, or mandates for low-carbon fuels in certain industries. International standards and guidelines are also being developed to ensure safety and quality of green hydrogen systems.
ai.risks: Technological risks associated with scaling up electrolyzer capacity and integrating renewable energy sources. Economic risks due to the high upfront costs and potential volatility in energy prices. Environmental risks from emissions during manufacturing processes unless strict controls are implemented.
ai.profitability: Profitability is currently limited by higher production costs compared to grey or blue hydrogen (produced via fossil fuels). However, as technology improves and renewable energy becomes cheaper, green hydrogen could become more competitive. Government subsidies can also enhance profitability in the short term.
ai.futureDevelopment: Ongoing research aims to improve efficiency of electrolysis processes, reduce costs through economies of scale, and develop better integration with existing infrastructure. Innovations such as solid-oxide electrolyzers are being explored for their potential to further decrease costs and increase performance.

glossary.def: The process of using an electric current to split water into hydrogen and oxygen.
Hydrogen produced from renewable energy sources, emitting no greenhouse gases during production.
Energy derived from natural resources that are replenished over short periods of time, such as wind or solar power.

subsystems.name: Renewable power supply
subsystems.role: provides the electricity that makes the hydrogen 'green'.

subsystems.name: Water treatment
subsystems.role: electrolysers need very pure water — usually about 9–10 litres per kilogram of hydrogen.

subsystems.name: Electrolyser stack
subsystems.role: splits water into hydrogen and oxygen using electricity.

subsystems.name: Power electronics
subsystems.role: converts AC grid power into the controlled DC the stack needs, and follows the variable output of the renewables.

subsystems.name: Gas processing
subsystems.role: cleans, dries and compresses the hydrogen to pipeline or storage pressure.

subsystems.name: Storage and transport
parts: salt cavern or lined rock cavern
liquefaction or ammonia conversion for export

subsystems.name: Balance of plant
subsystems.role: keeps the plant safe and efficient.

buildSteps.title: Choose the site
buildSteps.detail: Co-locate with cheap, firm renewables — often a windy or sunny coast with a port, and somewhere hydrogen can be used rather than shipped.

buildSteps.title: Build the power supply
buildSteps.detail: Install the wind or solar farm and the substation; coastal sites may add a desalination plant.

buildSteps.title: Make the water ultrapure
buildSteps.detail: Filter, desalinate and deionise the feed water so dissolved salts do not poison the stack.

buildSteps.title: Manufacture the stacks
buildSteps.detail: Catalyst is coated onto electrodes, membranes are sandwiched between plates, and hundreds of cells are stacked and sealed — a precision factory job, not a field job.

buildSteps.title: Install and wire the plant
buildSteps.detail: Stacks are bolted onto skids in modules; rectifiers, compressors and cooling are connected.

buildSteps.title: Commission
buildSteps.detail: Stacks are conditioned, leak-tested and run up while the control system learns to follow an intermittent power supply.

buildSteps.title: Compress and store
buildSteps.detail: Hydrogen is dried, compressed and pushed into tubes, caverns or a pipeline.

buildSteps.title: Link to offtake
buildSteps.detail: Connect to the refinery, ammonia plant, steel plant or filling station that will use it.

prerequisites.why: electricity is the dominant cost of green hydrogen, so it only competes where power is cheap and abundant.
alkaline and PEM machines are sold today, but supply chains and gigawatt-scale manufacturing are only now being built.
PEM stacks use iridium, one of the scarcest metals, so reducing or recycling it limits how fast the industry can grow.
most industrial demand is far from the best wind and sun; without cheap storage and transport the fuel cannot reach it.
customers must convert furnaces, ammonia plants or fleets to run on hydrogen instead of natural gas.

pathway.milestone: small and medium plants supplying refineries, ammonia and bus or truck fleets
pathway.unlocks: proof that electrolysers can run on variable renewable power.

pathway.milestone: multi-hundred-megawatt to gigawatt projects, including offshore wind feeding electrolysers at sea or on the coast
pathway.unlocks: costs falling toward fossil hydrogen through scale and mass manufacturing.

pathway.milestone: dedicated hydrogen pipelines and large salt-cavern storage
pathway.unlocks: turning intermittent renewable output into firm, deliverable fuel.

pathway.milestone: green ammonia and direct-reduced iron at industrial scale
pathway.unlocks: fertiliser, shipping fuel and low-carbon steel — the largest potential markets.
